title: Justification and Adoption
summary: How guilty sinners are declared righteous before God and welcomed into His family as sons and daughters.
description: Justification answers the question, "How can a sinner be right with a holy God?" Adoption answers, "How can a rebel become God's child?" This course explains justification by grace through faith in Christ, the meaning of imputed righteousness, the Reformation debate and its fair presentation, the harmony of Paul and James, and the rich privileges of adoption into God's family.
objectives: Define justification as God's legal declaration
Explain the ground, means and result of justification
Present the Protestant and Roman Catholic views fairly
Explain adoption and its privileges and responsibilities
outcomes: Explain justification by faith alone with key texts
Explain imputation and Abraham as the model of faith
Apply justification and adoption to assurance and daily life

modules.title: Right with God
modules.intro: Justification is a word from the law court. This week we see what it means for God to justify the ungodly.

lessons.title: A legal declaration
lessons.body:
To **justify** means to declare righteous, not to make righteous. It is the verdict of a judge. "If there be a controversy between men, and they come unto judgment... then they shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked" (Deuteronomy 25:1).

The astonishing gospel is that God "justifieth the ungodly" (Romans 4:5). The guilty are declared not guilty and righteous in His sight.

Job asked, "how should man be just with God?" (Job 9:2). Justification is God's answer: "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (Romans 3:24).

lessons.title: The ground: Christ's righteousness
lessons.body:
God does not simply ignore sin; He justifies on the basis of Christ's work. Our sins were counted to Christ, and His righteousness is counted to us. This is called **imputation**.

"For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Paul wanted to be "found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ" (Philippians 3:9).

The prophet called the Messiah "THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS" (Jeremiah 23:6). Our standing rests on what He has done.

lessons.title: The result: peace and no condemnation
lessons.body:
"Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 5:1). The war is over.

Justification is complete and final: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). "Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth" (8:33).

This does not depend on how we feel on a given day. A newly converted believer is as fully justified as a mature saint, because both stand in Christ's righteousness, not their own.

terms.def: God's legal declaration that a sinner is righteous in His sight through Christ.
To pronounce a verdict of righteousness, as a judge does, rather than to change a person's nature.
Counting or crediting one person's record to another.
Christ's righteousness credited to the believer's account.
The believer's freedom from God's sentence of judgement (Romans 8:1).
Jeremiah's title for the Messiah, Jehovah Tsidkenu (Jeremiah 23:6).

texts.teaches: God justifies the ungodly who believe.
Believers are justified freely by His grace through redemption in Christ.
Paul wanted the righteousness which is through faith in Christ, not his own.
Justified by faith, we have peace with God.
There is now no condemnation to those in Christ Jesus.

summary: Justification is God's legal verdict declaring sinners righteous.
Its ground is Christ's righteousness imputed to us.
It brings peace with God and no condemnation.
It is complete and does not vary with our feelings.

modules.title: By Faith Alone
modules.intro: How do we receive justification? This week we study faith as the means, Abraham as the example, and Paul and James together.

lessons.title: Abraham believed God
lessons.body:
Paul uses Abraham to show how justification works. "Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness" (Romans 4:3, quoting Genesis 15:6).

Abraham was justified before he was circumcised (Romans 4:10) and long before the law of Moses. So justification is not by rituals or law-keeping.

David also describes "the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works": "Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven" (Romans 4:6-7, quoting Psalm 32:1-2). Faith is the empty hand that receives God's gift.

lessons.title: Not by works of the law
lessons.body:
Paul is emphatic: "a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ" (Galatians 2:16). "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law" (Romans 3:28).

Why? Because "by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight" (Romans 3:20); the law exposes sin rather than removing it. And because salvation by works would allow boasting (Romans 3:27; Ephesians 2:9).

In Galatia, teachers added circumcision to faith. Paul called it "another gospel" (Galatians 1:6-9). Adding anything to Christ subtracts from grace.

lessons.title: Paul, James and living faith
lessons.body:
James writes, "Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only" (James 2:24). Does this contradict Paul?

No. They answer different questions. Paul asks how a sinner becomes right with God: by faith, apart from works. James asks how true faith is shown: by works. James attacks a dead, empty faith that says the right words but does nothing (2:14-17).

James' example is Abraham offering Isaac (2:21), which happened years after Genesis 15:6; it showed that his faith was real. The Reformers summarised it: "We are justified by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone."

terms.def: Reckoned or credited as righteousness, as with Abraham's faith (Genesis 15:6).
Obedience to the law of Moses offered as a basis for acceptance with God.
Latin for 'by faith alone': the Reformation teaching that justification is received by faith alone.
Paul's point that justification by faith leaves no room for human pride (Romans 3:27).
Paul's term for adding works such as circumcision to faith in Christ (Galatians 1:6).
Genuine faith that shows itself in obedience and good works.

texts.teaches: Abraham believed the LORD, and He counted it to him for righteousness.
A man is not justified by the works of the law but by faith in Christ.
A man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
By works a man is justified, and not by faith only, showing faith is real.
Believers are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.

summary: Abraham was justified by faith before circumcision and the law.
No one is justified by works of the law; boasting is excluded.
Paul and James agree: faith alone justifies, and living faith works.
Adding works to Christ is another gospel.

modules.title: Justification and the Reformation
modules.intro: Justification was at the centre of the Reformation. This week we present the main positions fairly and distinguish justification from sanctification.

lessons.title: Luther's discovery
lessons.body:
Martin Luther, a monk in Germany, tried hard to earn God's favour but found no peace. Studying Romans 1:17, "The just shall live by faith," he came to see that the righteousness of God is a gift received by faith, not a standard we must reach.

Luther said this truth opened the gates of paradise to him. Along with other Reformers such as Calvin, he taught that justification is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone.

This became a defining belief of Protestant churches, including Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal and Holiness churches today.

lessons.title: The Roman Catholic view
lessons.body:
The Roman Catholic Church, at the Council of Trent (1545-1563), taught that justification is a process in which God's grace is **infused** into the believer through faith and the sacraments, especially baptism, making the person inwardly righteous. Grace can be increased by good works and lost by mortal sin, then restored through the sacrament of penance.

Catholics stress that this is all by grace and that faith is necessary. They point to James 2:24 and to texts about being made new.

Protestants reply that Scripture treats justification as a declaration (Romans 8:33), based on Christ's imputed righteousness, complete at once. Both sides agree on the need for grace and a changed life; they differ on the ground of our standing before God.

lessons.title: Justification and sanctification
lessons.body:
Justification and sanctification always go together but must not be confused.

| Justification | Sanctification |
|---|---|
| A legal declaration | An inner transformation |
| Changes our standing | Changes our condition |
| Complete at once | Grows over a lifetime |
| Christ's righteousness counted to us | The Spirit's work in us |

If we confuse them, we either lose assurance (thinking our standing depends on our progress) or lose holiness (thinking a changed life does not matter). Paul holds both: "ye are washed... ye are sanctified... ye are justified" (1 Corinthians 6:11).

terms.def: The sixteenth-century movement that recovered justification by faith and reformed the church.

terms.term: The just shall live by faith
terms.def: The words of Habakkuk 2:4, quoted in Romans 1:17, that transformed Luther.
The Roman Catholic council (1545-1563) that defined Catholic teaching on justification.
The Catholic teaching that God's grace is poured into the soul, making it inwardly righteous.
The Spirit's work of making believers holy in character and life.
Belonging to the law court; used of justification as a legal declaration.

texts.teaches: The just shall live by faith.
The just shall live by his faith.
It is God who justifies; no one can lay a charge against His elect.
Those seeking justification by the law have fallen from grace.
Believers are washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus.

summary: Luther rediscovered justification by faith through Romans 1:17.
Protestants teach justification as a declaration based on imputed righteousness.
Catholics teach justification as a process of infused grace through faith and sacraments.
Justification and sanctification belong together but differ.

modules.title: Children of God
modules.intro: Justification makes us right with the Judge; adoption brings us into the Father's family. This week we study the privileges of adoption.

lessons.title: Brought into the family
lessons.body:
"Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God" (1 John 3:1).

In the Roman world, adoption gave a person a new name, a new father, full rights and full inheritance. Paul uses this picture: God sent His Son "to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons" (Galatians 4:4-5).

Adoption is God's act of grace, received by faith: "ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:26). Not everyone is God's child in this sense; it is the privilege of believers (John 1:12).

lessons.title: The privileges of sons and daughters
lessons.body:
Adoption brings great privileges:

- **Access**: we cry "Abba, Father" (Romans 8:15) and come boldly in prayer.
- **Assurance**: "The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God" (Romans 8:16).
- **Inheritance**: "if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ" (Romans 8:17).
- **Provision**: "your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things" (Matthew 6:32).
- **Loving discipline**: "whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth" (Hebrews 12:6).
- **A family**: believers are brothers and sisters (Mark 3:35).

lessons.title: Living as God's children
lessons.body:
Children should resemble their Father. "Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children" (Ephesians 5:1). "Every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself" (1 John 3:3).

Adoption also frees us from fear. We did not receive "the spirit of bondage again to fear" (Romans 8:15). God's children need not fear witchcraft, curses or the future, because their Father is sovereign and loving.

Adoption shapes the church too. In God's family, tribe, status and wealth do not divide: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free... for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28).

terms.def: God's act of bringing believers into His family as His sons and daughters.
An Aramaic word for Father, expressing close, trusting relationship.
Believers as those who will inherit all God has promised, with Christ.
Sharing Christ's inheritance as fellow heirs (Romans 8:17).
The Father's loving discipline that trains His children in holiness.
Slavish fear, which believers have not received (Romans 8:15).

texts.teaches: The Father's love makes believers called the sons of God.
Christ redeemed us that we might receive the adoption of sons.
God's children are heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ.
Whom the Lord loves He chastens.
All believers are one in Christ, whatever their background.

summary: Adoption brings believers into God's family with full rights.
Privileges include access, assurance, inheritance, provision and discipline.
God's children should resemble their Father in holiness.
Adoption frees us from fear and unites us across every division.

assignments.title: Peace with God
assignments.prompt: A believer tells you, "Some days I feel saved, other days I don't." Write a pastoral letter explaining justification, imputed righteousness and adoption, showing why their standing does not depend on feelings. Use at least five passages from the course.

assignments.title: Paul and James
assignments.prompt: Explain carefully how Romans 3-4 and James 2 fit together. Show what question each writer is answering, how each uses Abraham, and what this means for how we preach faith and good works.
